semantic_correction.stem: A client with a lower-leg fracture in a cast develops rapidly increasing pain that is not relieved by the prescribed analgesic, numbness in the foot, and marked pain when the toes are passively moved. A distal pulse is still palpable. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Treat the findings as possible acute compartment syndrome, urgently notify the surgical team, and continue focused neurovascular assessment.
options.B: Give the prescribed analgesic and reassess before notifying the surgical team because a palpable distal pulse argues against urgent ischemia.
options.C: Elevate the extremity well above heart level and continue routine cast checks unless pallor or loss of the distal pulse develops.
options.D: Document the symptoms as expected after a fracture and wait for the next scheduled neurovascular assessment before escalating care.

semantic_correction.rationale: Acute compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency in which increased compartment pressure can impair circulation and cause ischemic tissue injury. NCBI/StatPearls describes severe pain out of proportion to the injury, pain with passive stretch and paresthesia or sensory change as important findings and notes that palpable pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome; pulselessness, pallor and paralysis are typically late findings. Current NCBI WebM&M guidance likewise emphasizes escalating pain, pain with passive stretch and sensory changes and warns that preserved distal pulses do not rule out the diagnosis. The 2026 NCSBN NCLEX-RN Test Plan requires focused assessment, recognition of changes in condition and intervention to prevent complications. Option A recognizes the high-risk pattern and escalates urgently while continuing neurovascular assessment. B and C incorrectly use the palpable pulse or later ischemic signs to delay escalation; D misclassifies progressive neurovascular warning findings as expected recovery. Therefore A is the uniquely best answer.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Recognize escalating pain, pain with passive stretch and new sensory changes after an extremity injury or casting as possible acute compartment syndrome that requires urgent escalation even when a distal pulse remains palpable.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: retired a CMS value-based-purchasing/IPPS payment item because it tested health-policy finance trivia rather than entry-level nursing practice. Rebuilt the UID into recognition and urgent escalation of a possible acute compartment syndrome after lower-leg fracture/casting.

audit_findings_append.finding: The replacement tests a time-sensitive neurovascular complication relevant to entry-level RN assessment and escalation. No compartment-pressure threshold, fixed timing window or treatment dose is asserted.

scope_exclusions.pressure_threshold: No intracompartmental pressure number or diagnostic cutoff is used. The item tests clinical recognition and urgent escalation rather than pressure-based diagnosis.
scope_exclusions.definitive_diagnosis: The nurse is not asked to diagnose compartment syndrome definitively; the answer explicitly treats the findings as possible compartment syndrome requiring urgent escalation.
scope_exclusions.cast_removal: The item does not direct the nurse to independently split or remove a cast, because the scope and process for relieving external restriction can depend on the clinical setting and authorized emergency management.
scope_exclusions.analgesic_dose_or_interval: No medication name, dose or timing interval is specified. Failure of the prescribed analgesic to relieve rapidly increasing pain is used only as a qualitative warning finding.
scope_exclusions.pulse_rule: A palpable distal pulse is included specifically to prevent the common error of using preserved pulses to rule out acute compartment syndrome.

near_duplicate_check.note: Targeted GitHub search for 'compartment syndrome passive stretch' returned no indexed repository match. No broad bank rescan was performed.

option_audit.A: Correct. The combination of progressive pain, passive-stretch pain and sensory change warrants urgent escalation for possible compartment syndrome even with a palpable pulse.
option_audit.B: Plausible because analgesia and reassessment are routine after fracture, but preserved pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome and these progressive findings should not wait for another analgesic response.
option_audit.C: Plausible because elevation is common for swelling, but waiting for pallor or pulse loss relies on late findings; marked elevation is also not the recommended response to suspected compartment syndrome.
option_audit.D: Plausible normalization error, but the progression of pain and sensory changes is not an expected stable cast finding and requires prompt escalation.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. A alone responds to the complete acute warning pattern without relying on late ischemic findings. B, C and D all delay escalation despite progressive pain, passive-stretch pain and sensory change.

cueing_check.note: Exact character counts were calculated from the stored strings. Correct option A is not uniquely longest; all four are realistic clinical action sequences.

blueprint_audit.entry_level_relevance: NCSBN Reduction of Risk Potential directly includes focused assessment, recognition of changing condition, prevention of complications and monitoring of casted extremities. The item tests an entry-level RN's recognition and escalation of a limb-threatening complication.
